100mw Outshining Loadshedding

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a Bold step in the right direction brings South Africa new hope

Unique Selling Point:
South Africans who are losing hope amidst the toughest power crisis in recent history, can breathe a sigh of relief. President Ramaphosa has a brand new plan that may see the end to load shedding and power cuts, forever.

Summary:
In a bold move that few expected, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced amendments to a law that may finally see the end of load shedding. Energy experts and industry leaders across the board in every sector of the economy welcomed the fact that all South Africans are now allowed to trade power privately without a license from NERSA. Although the allowed volume may only be up to 100mw, the announcement saw Ramaphosa lifting the threshold ten times higher than what his own minister of mineral resources allowed.

Further information:
D
It seems that Eskom’s complete control over the country’s energy generation may soon be a thing of the past. South Africans are now permitted to buy electricity from private suppliers. These negotiations can be between the buyer and the seller and there is thus no interference or profit share for Eskom.
Private suppliers are no longer forced to obtain a license from government to trade in energy up to 100mw.
Up to date, the ministry of mineral resources’ Gwede Mantashe has fought relentlessly against lifting the permitted threshold, arguing that it would hold negative financial implications for Eskom. In his budget speech in May, Mantashe lifted the threshold to 10mw permitted to be generated outside Eskom while industry leaders, mines and the agricultural sector pleaded for 50mw. Early June, President Ramaphosa trumped his own minister and raised the threshold to 100MW.

But what does this mean to South Africans?

It means that load shedding may soon be a distant memory in South Africa’s history. The reason for this is simple: if large industry such as mines seize to drain the grid with their heavy energy demands, there will be enough power for small businesses and households to fully function. This paves the way for small business to enter the market as the price of electricity may inevitably drop drastically.

It is common knowledge for most South Africans that the majority of the country’s municipalities are in deep seeded debt with Eskom and that consumers bear the brunt. This may soon be over as consumers are no longer going to pay for Eskom’s shortfalls once the private energy sector is flourishing.

Private companies providing green energy, generated by wind, solar and water have always been looked to for solutions, but exasperated licensing right that have to be obtained from NERSA have slowed the process down and brought no solutions. But now, these companies and other wanting to enter the market can trade privately. They no longer have to ask permission from NERSA, the regulator holding the grip on the monopoly of power supply so tightly that it’s choking the South African economy.

Currently, Eskom is only lighting up 85% of South Africa, which means that 15% of the population have no electricity. The increased electricity regulation threshold may result in Eskom being able to light up this 15% of households in the population for the very first time.
This all form part of the roadmap going forward. Although it may not be an easy and quick journey, privatising electricity is the only option government has in providing solutions to fix the mess that is Eskom.

Press Release:


So Long Loadshedding?
For the first time in history, the entire South Africa may be lit up. Eskom has never been able to provide power to 100% of the population. And while the state-owned enterprise battled to keep existing lights on, it has been unable to spend the time and energy needed to resurrect its dilapidated coal fired power stations. That may all change now that President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a change in legislation that the private sector has been begging for, for years. The amended regulation will mobilise independent energy companies to generate power and sell it privately without having to jump bureaucratic licensing hoops at the National Energy Regulator of South Africa (NERSA). Until now, these companies were only allowed to generate one megawatt without a license, and those who wanted to build larger plants had to wait years for approval. NERSA’s licensing process blocked the renewable energy sector from developing and resulted in South Africa lagging behind the rest of the world. The new regulations will allow private companies to generate up to 100 megawatts each, enough to provide electricity to nearly a hundred thousand houses. Although these companies still have to undergo registration processes at NERSA and various other state entities, industry leaders believe it’s the first step in the right direction.

Script:


OUTSHINING LOADSHEDDING
VO
Load shedding may soon be thing of the past as government will now allow South Africans to produce and sell up to 100 megawatts without needing a license from NERSA. Private citizens or companies can erect various plants of 100 megawatts each. The president’s announcement on the amendment of electricity regulation brings great relief to an industry in crisis. Private renewable energy provider, Gareth Warner, says the announcement is a game changer.
SUPER@ GARETH WARNER: PRIVATE ENERGY SUPPLIER
“What it does mean particularly for South African business and large power users in South Africa that they are able to buy power from private suppliers these embedded power producers like myself and instead of following the long bureaucratic NERSA process, that frees it up. You don’t need a license you just need to register, as I understand it with NERSA”
VO
Up to this point, private providers were only allowed to produce 1MW without having to obtain a license from the electricity regulator NERSA. Now a hundredfold increase in the threshold will allow private players to generate 100 MW without a license. This will bring great relief to Eskom.

LINK
While struggling to keep the lights on, Eskom’s capacity to repair its power stations lagged behind, resulting in load shedding for the paying consumer. If the private sector can assist in helping to carry the burden of South Africa’s electricity supply, the state owned enterprise may be able to resurrect its derelict power generating plants.
VO
Currently, Eskom’s coal fired power stations carry a gigantic load according to chief economist of the Minerals Council South Africa Henk Langenhoven.
SUPER@ HENK LANGENHOVEN: CHIEF ECONOMIST: MINERALS COUNCIL SOUTH AFRICA
“Our evening peaks are massive, it is literally a power station or two that we need extra in the evening…this relief is virtually, I mean the numbers that we hear are in the order of 5000 megawatt. This is a power station!”

VO
The new regulation will mean that if private companies or individuals set up 50 plants of 100 megawatts each, the strain on the national grid can be relieved which means more electricity will be freed up. This is because
large industries like mines, pull massive volumes of power from the national grid and additional electricity will therefore bring much needed relief.
SUPER@ HENK LANGENHOVEN: CHIEF ECONOMIST: MINERALS COUNCIL SOUTH AFRICA
“Many of the mining are using two to three hundred megawatts so this is not to replace Eskom at all, we can’t replace Eskom. But it is to give us a 20-30 percent margin.”

VO
If a license is not required to erect power plants up to 100 megawatts, private companies may erect various such plants. But just how much power is 100 megawatts?
SUPER@ GARETH WARNER: PRIVATE ENERGY SUPPLIER
6’40-7’10”
“That is always an interesting question because different households use different electricity like if you use aircons obviously, consumption is higher. So rule of thumb, a 100Mw plant would equate to a 80 to 100 thousand homes. If you take Soweto for example, there are about 350 thousand homes in Soweto, you looking at three to four of that 100MW solar plants to provide power to a city of that size”.

VO
Experts say more electricity will result in overall economic growth. New businesses have to get energy approvals to operate. This could take years says Joanne Dean, vice chair of the South African renewable energy council.

SUPER@ JOANNE DEAN: VICE CHAIRPERSON: SAREC

“There are so many businesses that want to establish, and they cannot get access for power.
BACK TO BACK
“If you walk into the planning division of any electricity department of any utility and you walk into the gentleman’s office, you’ll see behind them files stacked behind him and those are applications for energy supply. So, none of these businesses are evolving and the small business are throttled and frustrated”

VO
Dean who also plays an advisory role to the ministry of minerals and mining, says, the impact of this decision made by president Ramaphosa affects all South Africans and not only large corporations.

SUPER@ JOANNE DEAN: VICE CHAIRPERSON: SAREC
“He made this wonderful announcement for this sector, and I don’t think the people have really understood the enormity of what it means for South Africa”

VO
But it may be a while for results to show.

MAC: “Jo another thing is that a plant can’t be erected overnight so a lot of people may argue that it may still take two years before we see any fruit. So, what happens in that matter? Will we still be faced with loadshedding?

JAONNE
“Indeed, we will.”

MAC:
That is not good!”

JOANNE
“The fact is that we waited a long time for this type of project to kick off. So if I can give you scale, you one megawatts and five megawatts and ten megawatts, those projects can get up really quickly form a four month to six month period so you might see that space really rocket. But if we look at that 50 to a hundred-megawatt projects can take anything from 18-24 months to build”

VO
Dean says, there are renewable plants able to deliver up to 5000 megawatts, ready and waiting in the pipeline.
South Africa has the climate and space to allow the development of green energy. Agricultural economist Kulani Siweya says many farmers will come to the party.

SUPER@ KULANI SIWEYA: AGRICULTURAL ECONOMIST: AGRISA
“The ability is there given that there is vast land where these energy plants can be set up. But moreover, and which is more important is that there is also private capital that is readily available to build these plants that will alleviate the pressure from Eskom”

VO

Although the new regulations will not allow surplus electricity to be pumped back into the Eskom grid, the additional energy may result in opening the economy to create more jobs. Langenhoven says, various mining employment opportunities are pending and may now come to fruition.
SUPER@ HENK LANGENHOVEN: CHIEF ECONOMIST: MINERALS COUNCIL SA
“We think that there are between 30 and 40 billion of mining projects, other projects, not electricity projects in the pipeline. If the electricity constraint disappears over time, the quicker it happens the better, then we are talking virtually talking the combination of the energy and the mining sector and that is the only way we can create more employment and that is by expanding mining activity”

VO
Another benefit is massive savings on utility costs for large corporations.
SUPER@ HENK LANGENHOVEN: CHIEF ECONOMIST: MINERALS COUNCIL SA
“If you can take the latest technology and install that, it is in the order of 60-kilowatt hour. We are now paying 120 kilowatts for the Eskom power.”
BACK-TO-BACK
“So you can imagine the margins at which these mines are running, it literally can make a difference between being viable or not”.

VO
Freeing up the market will also result in cheaper tariffs for consumers and dropping the price of household solar instalation.

SUPER@ JOANNE DEAN: VICE CHAIRPERSON: SAREC
“Remember when cellphones first came out where your model is launched, is hell of a expansive and then it comes down as soon as there is bulk sales. Obviously, the cheaper the technology the cheaper the electricity”

VO
This, while Eskom will be able to now provide electricity to the poorest of the poor.

LINK
15% of South Africa has never been electrified by Eskom. The new regulations may mean that rural areas will have light for the first time in history.

SUPER@ JOANNE DEAN: VICE CHAIRPERSON: SAREC
“Eskom is still the de facto monopoly because it still needs to provide for the poorest of the poor. It still has to provide for the middle-income groups, and these are the people we don’t want to see be left behind.”

VO
The amended regulation will be gazette within 60 days of the president’s announcement and will have a further 30 days for comments. AGRISA says, although the license challenge is out of the way, it remains to be seen just what the new regulations will entail.

SUPER@KULANI SIWEYA: AGRICULTURAL ECONOMIST: AGRISA
“That particular amendment does not necessarily mean that the red tape is removed overnight. On the one side you have NERSA and they still need to develop the process as to how the registration of a 100mw project will still need to happen on that regard.”

VO
New projects will need environmental impact approval from government, but many key players say they already have that in place.


PROMOS

Surprising moves taken by the president to end load-shedding and prevent the country’s economy from collapsing. We bring you the ins and outs of new electricity regulations for private suppliers.

Unlocking the private sector to generate power will assist Eskom in carrying the burden and may bring an end to load shedding. We unpack new regulations that will allow private supply.

Adding additional electricity to the grid and mobilising the private sector to help will not only bring relief to consumers but growth for the entire economy and added job opportunities.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): a Bold step in the right direction brings South Africa new hope
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africans who are losing hope amidst the toughest power crisis in recent history, can breathe a sigh of relief. President Ramaphosa has a brand new plan that may see the end to load shedding and power cuts, forever.
metadata.Summary: In a bold move that few expected, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced amendments to a law that may finally see the end of load shedding. Energy experts and industry leaders across the board in every sector of the economy welcomed the fact that all South Africans are now allowed to trade power privately without a license from NERSA. Although the allowed volume may only be up to 100mw, the announcement saw Ramaphosa lifting the threshold ten times higher than what his own minister of mineral resources allowed.
metadata.Further information: D It seems that Eskom’s complete control over the country’s energy generation may soon be a thing of the past. South Africans are now permitted to buy electricity from private suppliers. These negotiations can be between the buyer and the seller and there is thus no interference or profit share for Eskom. Private suppliers are no longer forced to obtain a license from government to trade in energy up to 100mw. Up to date, the ministry of mineral resources’ Gwede Mantashe has fought relentlessly against lifting the permitted threshold, arguing that it would hold negative financial implications for Eskom. In his budget speech in May, Mantashe lifted the threshold to 10mw permitted to be generated outside Eskom while industry leaders, mines and the agricultural sector pleaded for 50mw. Early June, President Ramaphosa trumped his own minister and raised the threshold to 100MW. But what does this mean to South Africans? It means that load shedding may soon be a distant memory in South Africa’s history. The reason for this is simple: if large industry such as mines seize to drain the grid with their heavy energy demands, there will be enough power for small businesses and households to fully function. This paves the way for small business to enter the market as the price of electricity may inevitably drop drastically. It is common knowledge for most South Africans that the majority of the country’s municipalities are in deep seeded debt with Eskom and that consumers bear the brunt. This may soon be over as consumers are no longer going to pay for Eskom’s shortfalls once the private energy sector is flourishing. Private companies providing green energy, generated by wind, solar and water have always been looked to for solutions, but exasperated licensing right that have to be obtained from NERSA have slowed the process down and brought no solutions. But now, these companies and other wanting to enter the market can trade privately. They no longer have to ask permission from NERSA, the regulator holding the grip on the monopoly of power supply so tightly that it’s choking the South African economy. Currently, Eskom is only lighting up 85% of South Africa, which means that 15% of the population have no electricity. The increased electricity regulation threshold may result in Eskom being able to light up this 15% of households in the population for the very first time. This all form part of the roadmap going forward. Although it may not be an easy and quick journey, privatising electricity is the only option government has in providing solutions to fix the mess that is Eskom.
